intro:
Chapter 45 stops introducing new mechanisms and instead makes the previous twenty-odd chapters agree with each other. The exercises trace one unit of work from an HTTP request, through canonicalization and a verification root, into an owned task envelope on a broker, out to a worker pool that routes graph and matrix workloads onto separate lanes, and finally to a durable finish-once result. Every question is really the same question asked at a different boundary: who owns this value here, and what happens to it when a process crashes mid-flight.

The solutions below commit to concrete owners rather than component names. The recurring rule is that the queue carries an owned envelope (never a borrow into request-local state), duplicate suppression lives at the durable completion boundary (not in a fragile local cache), and the verification gate runs before the expensive side effect (never after). The lab assembles these rules into a small verified dispatcher you can compile and run.

exerciseSolutions.title: Assemble the capstone architecture from earlier chapters
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk the sentence left to right and label each arrow as either an async runtime boundary (inside one process, the Tokio scheduler hands work between tasks) or a transport boundary (the message physically leaves this process and lands in a broker or queue). `HTTP request -> canonicalize -> compute verification root -> publish task` is all inside the API process: those are Tokio task boundaries, awaits on futures that share an address space. `publish -> claim` is the broker boundary: the envelope is serialized, leaves the API process, and is later claimed by an unrelated worker process. `claim -> execute -> durable completion -> notify` is again mostly in-process for one worker, with the durable-completion write being a boundary out to a store that other processes can read.

The task first has to become fully owned at the publish boundary. Before that, the request handler is allowed to borrow request-local buffers, headers, and connection state. At the moment of `publish`, the work is about to outlive the request that created it, so it must be an owned `TaskEnvelope` with owned fields (an owned id, owned tenant, an owned verification root, an owned workload) and no `&'a` borrow into the HTTP request. The chapter's first code sample is exactly this envelope.

Duplicate suppression and finish-once state belong to the durable completion subsystem, the same store that records the authoritative result, keyed by task id (or attempt-independent idempotency key). It cannot live only in a worker's in-memory cache, because the failure that produces duplicates, a lease expiring while a worker is slow or partitioned, is precisely the failure that erases that cache. Putting finish-once at the durable boundary is what makes a replay harmless: the second writer observes the first completion and becomes a no-op.

The graph, matrix, and accelerator lanes enter after `claim`, downstream of the dispatcher, on the execution side only. The dispatcher stays thin: it verifies and decodes one delivery, then sends the decoded spec down a workload-specific channel. Graph and matrix are separate executor lanes with separate budgets; the optional MPI or CUDA path is a swap of the matrix executor, not a change to the transport or verification lanes.
criteria: Owned boundary named: the publish step carries an owned TaskEnvelope; async boundary named: the awaits between canonicalize, compute-root, and publish are Tokio task boundaries.
Duplicate suppression placed at the durable completion store keyed by task id, explicitly not in a worker's in-memory cache that the failing lease destroys.
Execution lanes (graph, matrix, accelerator) separated from the transport (broker) and verification (root) lanes, sitting only downstream of claim.

exerciseSolutions.title: Review a flawed capstone delivery path
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Classify each defect as ownership, pacing, correctness, or observability, because the repairs are different in kind.

Ownership: the handler reaches into request state to build what it publishes. In the snippet the `req` is moved into the `async move` task, so `let body = &req.body` compiles, but the design is still wrong: the broker is handed a bare `&[u8]` borrowed out of the moved request rather than an owned, versioned envelope. The lifetime bug appears the moment the borrow is NOT owned by the task (drop the `move`, or derive `body` from request-local state that stays behind), and a spawned future must be `'static`. Either way the failure is the same: published work that depends on the request that created it. The repair is to build an owned `TaskEnvelope` before spawning or publishing, so the work owns everything it needs.

Pacing: one shared queue for all workloads couples fast and slow classes. A burst of slow matrix jobs sits ahead of fast graph jobs in the same FIFO, so a graph job's tail latency is now a function of matrix backlog it has nothing to do with. This is head-of-line blocking. The repair is to route by workload class into separate queues (the chapter's `tasks.graph` versus `tasks.matrix`) and give each lane its own worker budget, so a matrix backlog can grow without stalling graph work.

Correctness: ack-before-store acknowledges broker delivery before the durable result is written. If the worker crashes in the window between ack and store, the broker believes the work is done and will not redeliver, but no durable result exists. That is lost work, a correctness bug, not a telemetry gap. The repair is store-then-ack: write the durable completion (idempotently), and only then ack the broker. Combined with finish-once keying, a redelivery after a pre-ack crash re-executes safely and the duplicate completion collapses.

Observability and replay: the envelope records no trace id and no dedupe/idempotency key. Without a dedupe key, store-then-ack cannot suppress the duplicate it is designed to tolerate; without a trace id, you cannot follow one task across the API, broker, and worker hops when you are debugging the incident. The repair is to add a stable idempotency key (task id or attempt-independent key) and a trace/correlation id to the envelope contract, since these must be present at publish time, not bolted on at the worker.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Three repairs: own the envelope before spawn, route by workload, store-then-ack with a dedupe key.
criteria: At least three concrete failures named: borrowed request data into spawned work, one shared queue, ack-before-store, and missing trace/dedupe fields.

One per category explained: ownership (the broker is handed a borrow into request state instead of an owned envelope), pacing (shared-queue head-of-line blocking), correctness (ack-before-store loses work on crash).
A repair given for each: build an owned envelope, split queues by route, store-then-ack with idempotency, and add trace id plus dedupe key to the contract.

exerciseSolutions.title: Define implementation milestones and acceptance criteria
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Four milestones, each with a single binary completion condition another engineer can check, a test lane, and a telemetry prerequisite for the next step. The one decision that must not move across all four is the task envelope shape, the durable contract.

Milestone 1, single-process reference. Done when one process accepts a request, canonicalizes it, computes a verification root, runs the graph and matrix workloads in-process, and prints or stores a durable result, with the `TaskEnvelope` type already final. Tests: unit tests for canonicalization, root computation, and each executor; a small end-to-end integration test through the in-process path. Telemetry before moving on: per-request latency and a completion counter, so milestone 2 has a baseline.

Milestone 2, brokered path. Done when publish and claim go through the real broker, the worker is a separate process, and completion is store-then-ack with finish-once keying. The envelope on the wire is byte-identical to milestone 1's type. Tests: integration tests across the broker; a replay test that redelivers one task and asserts exactly one durable completion. Telemetry before moving on: queue age (publish-to-claim), retry/redelivery rate, and durable-completion lag.

Milestone 3, specialized worker lanes. Done when graph and matrix have separate queues and separate worker budgets, and the matrix lane can swap a CPU, MPI, or CUDA executor behind the same outer contract. Tests: a per-lane integration test; a soak test that bursts matrix jobs and asserts graph p99 stays flat (the isolation proof). Telemetry before moving on: per-lane queue age and per-lane utilization, plus accelerator-lane admission.

Milestone 4, production rollout hardening. Done when the service ships with canary, rollback artifacts, bounded local queues, and an explicit replay-after-crash policy. Tests: a soak test under sustained load and a chaos/crash test that kills a worker mid-execution and asserts no lost or duplicated completion. Telemetry: the rollout gates themselves (queue age, retry rate, verification failures, durable-completion lag) must be wired before promotion.
criteria: Four milestones defined (single-process, brokered, specialized lanes, rollout hardening), each with one clear completion condition.
A test or verification lane attached to each: unit+integration, integration+replay, per-lane+soak, soak+chaos/crash.
The TaskEnvelope shape is held stable as the durable contract from milestone 1 onward, frozen earlier than the executor internals.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair worker idempotency and queue budgets
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Two symptoms, two distinct repairs: duplicate completions during lease expiry is a correctness bug; queue-age spikes on matrix bursts is a pacing bug. Fix correctness first, then pacing.

Finish-once state must live in the durable completion store, the single durable owner, keyed by the task's idempotency key and written with a conditional put (put-if-absent or compare-and-set on a completion marker), then acked only after the durable write succeeds. A lease expires when a worker is merely slow or partitioned, not dead; the broker redelivers, a second worker runs, and both try to complete. If finish-once lives in either worker's memory, neither sees the other, so the side effect duplicates. With the marker in the durable store, the second completion observes the first and becomes a no-op, which is what makes a replay harmless. Note that a put-if-absent helper that returns whether the stored result matches cannot tell you whether *this* call was the first writer; both the original and a same-result replay see a match. Never gate the side effect on that return value: gate it on the durable marker itself, and if you genuinely need to detect the first writer, use a compare-and-set that reports whether it performed the insert.

Graph and matrix should split into separate queues and separate worker pools. They have different service-time distributions; sharing one FIFO means a matrix burst sits in front of graph jobs and inflates graph queue age for no reason. Separate routes (`tasks.graph`, `tasks.matrix`) plus separate budgets let the matrix backlog grow in its own lane while graph latency stays flat. This is a pacing repair first and a throughput repair second.

The local in-process queues, the bounded channels feeding each executor lane, should be bounded, and admission should push back rather than buffer forever. When a lane is saturated, the bounded channel fills, the dispatcher's send awaits, and backpressure propagates up to the broker claim and ultimately to the admission permit at ingress, where it belongs. An unbounded local queue just relocates the outage into memory.

The regression test that proves the replay path is fixed: enqueue one task, force a redelivery (simulate lease expiry by delivering the same envelope twice, possibly concurrently), and assert that the durable store contains exactly one completion and that the externally visible side effect happened exactly once. Run it both sequentially and with the two deliveries racing, since the racing case is the one that exposes a non-atomic put-if-absent.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Finish-once lives in the durable store via put-if-absent; complete_once reports whether the result matches, not who wrote first, so the side effect is gated on the durable marker, not this return value. Sequential and racing tests prove replay collapses to one completion.
criteria: Idempotent completion placed in one durable owner (the completion store) via put-if-absent keyed by task id.
Slow matrix class isolated from fast graph class via separate queues and worker pools.
Bounded local channels named, with admission pushing back to ingress instead of buffering unboundedly.
A replay test defined: deliver the same envelope twice (sequentially and racing) and assert exactly one durable completion and one side effect.

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile and refactor the capstone from evidence
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the numbers before touching a kernel. Queue p95 is 800 ms while worker run time is 70 ms: the work spends roughly eleven times longer waiting in line than it does executing. The dominant bottleneck is queueing and accelerator admission, not local handler CPU. A 70 ms handler is not the first thing to optimize when items wait 800 ms to start.

The metric that should have paged first is queue age (publish-to-claim wait), not error rate and not handler CPU. The next trace to inspect is a single slow task's span timeline: the gap between enqueue and dequeue confirms the wait is in the queue, and per-lane breakdown shows whether the wait is concentrated in the saturated accelerator lane. The evidence already points there: one accelerator lane is saturated while CPU graph workers sit mostly idle, so capacity is mis-allocated across lanes.

The retry rate of 25% of deliveries belongs in the capacity story, not only the error story. A quarter of work being retried is amplifying offered load by about 25 percent, which feeds the very queue that is already backed up. So before any graph or matrix kernel optimization, the refactor is to relieve the queueing pressure: split or rebalance the lanes so the saturated accelerator lane gets admission control and the idle CPU graph workers either take overflow (where the workload allows a CPU fallback) or are rebalanced, and classify retries so that non-retriable failures stop being re-enqueued. Kernel tuning would shave milliseconds off a 70 ms run while the 800 ms wait remains untouched.

Before-and-after signals that prove the repair moved the real bottleneck: queue p95 should fall toward the worker run time (a few times 70 ms, not 800 ms), and accelerator-lane utilization should drop out of saturation while CPU-graph utilization rises, showing the load rebalanced. A second confirming signal is retry rate falling after retry classification, and a third is that end-to-end p99 tracks queue age down rather than staying pinned, confirming queue wait, not execution, was the dominant term.
criteria: Queueing / accelerator admission identified as the dominant story (800 ms wait vs 70 ms run), not local handler CPU.
One metric (queue age) and one trace field (per-lane enqueue-to-dequeue span / lane utilization) chosen for the next diagnostic step.
One evidence-tied refactor proposed: lane split/rebalance with accelerator admission control plus retry classification, before any kernel work.
At least two validation signals named: queue p95 falling toward run time, accelerator utilization leaving saturation (plus retry rate and p99 as further confirmation).

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose rollout, acceleration, and failure isolation policy
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Make the fallback boring and explicit. The stable fallback is the CPU-only execution path: it has no external toolchain dependency, no device to be unavailable, and the most predictable failure modes. The selection rule is to prefer a specialist lane (MPI or CUDA) only when it is healthy and the batch is dense enough to pay for it, and to fall back to CPU automatically when the specialist lane is saturated, unavailable, or failing its health check. Specialist acceleration is an optimization layered on top of a path that always works, never the only way to make progress.

During canary, the active lane must be visible, not inferred. Expose the build/version artifact id, the executor selection knobs (which lanes are enabled, the dense-batch threshold, the per-lane concurrency cap), and a per-task label recording which lane actually ran it. Operators need to read, from telemetry alone, which lane is active for the canary cohort without attaching a debugger.

Isolate retry storms by giving each specialist lane its own queue, its own worker pool, and its own retry budget. A CUDA driver hiccup that storms retries must stay confined to the CUDA lane: its bounded queue fills, admission pushes back into that lane only, and graph and CPU-matrix work continue. Without that split, one specialist's retry storm becomes a system-wide load amplifier. Classify failures so that non-retriable errors (verification drift, malformed input) dead-letter immediately instead of being retried into the storm.

Promotion gates, tied to concrete telemetry: queue age (per lane) must stay within budget, retry rate must stay below threshold, verification-failure rate must be at or near zero, and durable-completion lag must stay bounded; canary error and latency p99 must match or beat the incumbent. All four must hold for a sustained window before broad rollout. The rollback artifact is the previous immutable build/image plus its pinned configuration, kept ready so the operator action during an incident is a one-step pin-back to the known-good artifact, not a rebuild from memory. A feature flag that forces CPU-only execution is the fast in-place mitigation while the rollback completes.
criteria: Safe fallback defined (CPU-only path) and a specialist selection rule (use MPI/CUDA only when healthy and batch is dense; auto-fall-back otherwise).
A failure-isolation mechanism included: per-lane queue, worker-pool, and retry-budget split confining a specialist retry storm.
At least two rollout gates tied to telemetry: queue age, retry rate, verification failures, durable-completion lag (all named, with thresholds for a sustained window).
A pre-built rollback artifact named (previous immutable image plus pinned config) plus a force-CPU flag, so the incident action is a pin-back, not a rebuild from memory.

labSolution.explanation:
This is the completed form of the exercise-page starter, so it reads back against the same expected output. The two stub functions are filled in: `should_run` returns `task.verified`, which is the control-path gate that keeps an unverified task from ever being dispatched, and `route` matches on the workload variant to return `tasks.graph` for `Workload::Graph` and `tasks.matrix` for `Workload::Matrix`. The gate runs before the route is recorded, mirroring the chapter's rule that verification comes before the expensive side effect.

The loop walks three tasks in order. `graph-1` is verified, so it is accepted and `last_route` becomes `tasks.graph`. `matrix-1` is verified, so it is accepted and `last_route` becomes `tasks.matrix`. `reject-1` is not verified, so it is rejected and `last_route` is left untouched. The final tallies are therefore `accepted = 2`, `rejected = 1`, and `last route = tasks.matrix`: two accepted, one rejected, and the last accepted task's route is the matrix route.

Keeping `route` as a pure function of the workload variant is what lets graph and matrix work be split onto separate broker keys (and later separate queues) without changing the outer task contract, matching the worker-pool example the chapter builds on.

reviewAnswers.question: Where should the capstone first cross from borrowed request data into an owned durable envelope?
reviewAnswers.answer: At the publish boundary, the moment work is about to leave the request that created it. Up to that point the handler may borrow request-local buffers and headers, but a published task can be claimed long after the HTTP request is gone, so it must be an owned TaskEnvelope with owned fields and no borrow into request state. Crossing into owned data here removes most async and retry lifetime confusion, because the spawned or published future no longer depends on anything tied to the request's lifetime.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should duplicate suppression live near durable completion rather than only in one in-memory worker cache?
reviewAnswers.answer: Duplicates arise precisely when a lease expires because a worker is slow or partitioned, and the broker redelivers to a second worker; that same failure also destroys any state in the first worker's memory. A per-worker cache cannot see the other worker, so both complete and the side effect duplicates. Keeping finish-once state in the durable completion store, keyed by an idempotency key and written with put-if-absent, lets the second completion observe the first and collapse to a no-op, which is what makes a replay harmless.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between profiling queue wait and profiling worker run time in this system?
reviewAnswers.answer: Queue wait (publish-to-claim age) measures how long work sits before any worker touches it and is dominated by capacity, admission, and lane allocation; worker run time measures how long execution takes once started and is dominated by the kernel and the executor. They demand different fixes: high queue wait calls for queue splits, worker-budget changes, admission control, and retry classification, while high run time calls for kernel and executor optimization. Confusing them wastes effort, as tuning a 70 ms kernel does nothing for an 800 ms queue wait.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should specialist graph, matrix, MPI, or CUDA lanes still preserve one stable outer task contract?
reviewAnswers.answer: The outer task envelope is the durable contract that the broker, the verification step, the completion store, and observability all depend on; the executor is an interior implementation detail. Keeping the envelope stable lets you swap a CPU executor for an MPI or CUDA one, split lanes, or rebalance budgets without rewriting transport, idempotency, or telemetry. If each specialist lane invented its own contract you would get contract drift, the exact failure mode where replay, acceleration, and observability stop agreeing with each other.

reviewAnswers.question: What makes an implementation milestone useful instead of decorative?
reviewAnswers.answer: A milestone is useful when another engineer can tell unambiguously whether it is done, which means one concrete completion condition plus a verification lane (a test) and the telemetry needed to start the next milestone. Decorative milestones describe activity without a checkable end state, so progress becomes a matter of opinion. The capstone plan also keeps the durable contract, the task envelope shape, frozen early and stable across milestones, so later work changes the executor internals rather than the contract every other process relies on.
